sentences.text: The name Limusaurus means mud lizard, and it is the only species within this extinct genus.
This animal possessed an elongated neck with long vertebrae similar to Elaphrosaurus, while its skull was short and roughly half the length of the femur.
Its jaws featured a beak that covered the tip of the lower jaw, a structure previously unknown in non-avian theropods.
As a very basal ceratosaurian, Limusaurus retained four fingers in its hand, though the first digit was strongly reduced.
Limusaurus ranks among the very few known jawed vertebrates to completely lose its teeth during its lifetime, representing the most extreme case of age-related dental change among dinosaurs.
It is considered the earliest known toothless theropod and the only non-bird theropod with strong bilateral reduction of its digits.
This creature is the first defined ceratosaurian discovered from East Asia and stands as one of the earliest members of the group.
Paleontologist Xu Xing and colleagues described and named the species Limusaurus inextricabilis in 2009 from fossils found in the Upper Shishugou Formation in the Junggar Basin of China.
One adult specimen of Limusaurus is estimated to be 15% larger than the holotype.
Limusaurus is notable for completely losing its teeth as it matured from juvenile to adult stages, which researchers interpreted as adaptations for a herbivorous diet.
The animal underwent a drastic transformation as it aged, losing its juvenile teeth and developing a beak, with studies indicating extreme anatomical changes during growth.
Fossil specimens exhibit 78 distinct anatomical changes associated with growth, causing juvenile specimens to group separately from adults.
Analysis of growth rings in 2017 determined that Limusaurus reached skeletal maturity at six years of age, a finding supported by histological analysis of growth lines in the tibiae.
The loss of teeth in adults likely indicated a dietary shift from omnivory to herbivory, supported by the presence of gastroliths that were larger and more numerous in older adults.

Adult specimens show herbivory-associated morphological traits shared with other herbivorous theropod groups like Ornithomimosauria, Therizinosauria, Oviraptorosauria, Alvarezsauroidea, and the troodontid Jinfengopteryx.

Paleontologists suggested that Limusaurus likely lived in groups based on the abundance of fossils and evidence of rapid burial, where large numbers of fossils in mud pits likely result from the tendency of small animals to get trapped.

Xu and colleagues classified Limusaurus as a basal member of Ceratosauria in 2009, noting it was the first known ceratosaur from Asia and belongs to the family Noasauridae, closely related to Elaphrosaurus.
The genus Limusaurus was named by Xu and colleagues in 2009.
Limusaurus lived during the Oxfordian stage of the Jurassic period, approximately 161 to 157 million years ago, in what is now Asia.

The pattern of digit reduction in Limusaurus supports a contested hypothesis regarding the evolution of the three-fingered hand in tetanuran theropods and birds. Researchers initially used Limusaurus to support the Bilateral Digit Reduction hypothesis regarding the evolution of bird hands, but it is possible that bilateral digit reduction occurred only in Ceratosauria and not in Tetanurae.
